summary: Kole Jain walks through four decorative Figma effects built from gradients, blend modes, inner shadows and blurs: a kaleidoscope effect, a clay effect, a metallic effect and plugin-free mesh gradients. For each he names where it fits: kaleidoscope for credit cards, stickers and buttons; clay for isometrics and illustrations that need depth; metallic for credit cards and metal mockups; mesh gradients for websites, posters and slideshows. The recipes hinge on a few load-bearing details, such as keeping the Screen layer on top in the kaleidoscope, avoiding saturated colors for clay, and needing a noticeable color change in the middle of the metallic gradient. For a design system, the video is a recipe book for decorative surfaces and brand illustration rather than for core UI, and he openly says the kaleidoscope's usability is poor even though it looks good.
key_ideas: Decorative effects in Figma can be built from layered gradients, blend modes (Difference, Screen, Overlay), inner shadows and blurs; only the kaleidoscope's optional noise step uses a plugin.

Each effect has named best uses: kaleidoscope for credit cards, stickers and buttons; clay for isometrics and illustrations; metallic for credit cards and metal mockups and 'not a whole lot else'; mesh gradients on websites, posters, slideshows and 'just about everything else'.
In the kaleidoscope, layer order is load-bearing: the Screen layer must sit on top of everything else or the effect breaks.
The kaleidoscope's angular gradient should alternate black and white an even number of times.
An effect can look good while being poor for usability; the kaleidoscope with overlay text is his own example.
The clay effect comes from two inner shadows, one covering the top and right edges and one the bottom and left, and it works poorly with saturated colors.
A metallic look needs a noticeable color change in the middle of the gradient; the edge colors matter less.
A white radial gradient on Overlay adds depth and thickness to a metallic surface.
A layer with a fill of 20% in a red, orange or blue turns plain metal into rose gold, gold, bronze or titanium.
Mesh gradients come from stacked, blurred, semi-transparent circles on Overlay; the more overlapping layers, the brighter and more vibrant the result.
Mesh gradients are more art than science: iterate on colors, blurs and transparencies until it looks right.

decisions.question: Which decorative effect fits this surface?

options.name: Kaleidoscope
options.effect: Striped radial pattern from the angular gradient, with noise and overlay text; looks good, but its usability is poor.

options.name: Clay
options.effect: Muted-color shape with inner shadows on opposite edges that gives it depth.
options.when: Isometrics or illustrations that need some depth.

options.name: Metallic
options.effect: Gray and dark blue sheen with a highlight and inner shadows that reads as a metal plate; can be tinted to rose gold, gold, bronze or titanium.
options.when: Credit cards and metal mockups, and not much else.

options.name: Mesh gradient
options.effect: Soft, blurred multi-color background that grows brighter and more vibrant with more layers.
options.when: Websites, posters, slideshows and most other surfaces.

decisions.recommendation: He calls the mesh gradient probably the most useful of the four and uses it on just about everything he can; the others have narrower use cases.
decisions.evidence: our last and probably most useful effect is creating mesh gradients

decisions.question: Should a metallic surface stay plain metal or be tinted?

options.effect: Grays and dark blues with an Overlay highlight and inner shadows.
options.when: The default metallic credit card or mockup.

options.name: Tinted metal
options.effect: An extra layer with a 20% fill in red, orange or blue gives a rose gold, gold, bronze or titanium feel.
options.when: When you want a specific finish such as rose gold.

decisions.evidence: now let's say we want our credit card to be rose gold

decisions.question: How vibrant should a mesh gradient be?

options.name: 8 to 10 or more overlapping layers
options.when: When you want a brighter, more vibrant gradient.

decisions.recommendation: Don't be afraid to use 8 to 10 layers or more, then tune colors, blurs and transparencies until you're happy.
decisions.evidence: the more layers you use that overlap the brighter and more vibrant your gradient will become

process.detail: Draw a circle with a radial gradient in any colors.
Add a layer with an angular gradient alternating black and white an even number of times (eight; 10 or six also work) and set it to Difference.
Duplicate the stripe layer, set the copy to Screen and keep it on top of everything else.
Add noise with the Noise & Texture plugin, then add thicker text set to Overlay.
Draw a rectangle in a non-saturated color, add one inner shadow covering the top and right edges and another covering the bottom and left edges, and optionally a drop shadow.
Draw a rounded rectangle with a linear gradient of mostly grays and dark blues with a noticeable change in the middle, add a white radial gradient layer on Overlay, then two inner shadows.
For rose gold, gold, bronze or titanium, add another layer with a 20% fill in a red, orange or blue.
Place a semi-transparent, blurred circle as the background, add more semi-transparent, blurred circles set to Overlay, repeat (8 to 10 layers or more), and tune colors, blurs and transparencies.

examples.visual_note: A radial-gradient circle overlaid with black and white angular stripes on Difference and Screen, plus noise and Overlay text; shows how layer order and blend modes create a radiating pattern for cards, stickers or buttons.
A muted-color rectangle with inner shadows on the top and right and on the bottom and left edges; shows how opposing inner shadows add depth for isometrics and illustrations.

examples.what: Metallic credit card, plus a rose gold variant
examples.visual_note: A rounded card with a gray and dark blue gradient, an Overlay white highlight and inner shadows, then a 20% colored fill layer to make it rose gold; shows how a mid-gradient color change and a tint layer read as metal.
Stacked blurred, semi-transparent circles on Overlay forming a soft multi-color gradient; shows that more overlapping layers make it brighter and more vibrant.

caveats: The inner-shadow, blur and transparency values are only shown on screen ('with these settings'); the transcript has no numbers for them, so the recipes can't be fully reproduced from text.
The kaleidoscope recap is shown on screen for viewers to screenshot and is not in the transcript.
Auto-caption says the blend mode is 'differ'; this is Figma's Difference blend mode. 'the colors of the rain' is probably 'the rainbow', but that is not certain.
These are decorative, Dribbble-style effects, not core UI guidance; he admits the kaleidoscope's usability is pretty bad.
The use cases for each effect are his opinion, not tested guidance.
Self-promotion: the Figma file is offered through a link in the pinned comment, and he asks for a thumbs up for a part two.
Published 2024-04-13; Figma's interface and the Noise & Texture plugin may have changed since.
Figma only: no CSS or code equivalents are covered.
